Saturday, 14 June. Julien and Karim are having a coffee on a terrace in the Presqu’île. In three weeks Julien leaves for Iași. He is very nervous.
Good morning, gentlemen. What can I get you?
I’d like a coffee, please. And could you bring us a glass of water?
A tea for me, thanks. (The waitress leaves.) Karim, I need your advice. In three weeks I’m meeting Ioana’s family.
Ah! The big moment! Are you nervous?
Very. What would you do in my place?
Me? I’d learn a few words of Romanian. Parents love that. When I met Leïla’s family, I learnt to say “thank you” in Arabic… with a terrible accent!
Radu is already teaching me a bit. But I’m not sure he’s teaching me the right words…
Ha ha! You should check with Ioana. And you should bring presents. If I were you, I’d take wine and cheese from Savoie.
Her father likes wine, that’s true. And her grandmother? What could I give her?
A grandmother who makes a list of dishes? She’d be happy if you ate everything. Twice.
There’s something else… I’d like to ask him something important. Her father, I mean.
Wait… You mean… you’d like to ask Ioana to marry you?
Shh! Not so loud! Yes. But not right away. I’d like to get to know her family first. It would be good to talk to her father first, wouldn’t it?
That would be very elegant. But in your place, I wouldn’t tell him anything before the third glass of țuică.
You think so? And what if her father said no?
If he knew you like I do, he’d say yes straight away. Come on, would you pay for the coffees to thank me?

Almost the same! The future “je ferai” ends in a closed é (“fuh-RAY”), the conditional “je ferais” in an open è (“fuh-REH”). Many French people don’t even make the difference any more; context helps.
“Zhuh voo-DREH”: the most useful word in French. With it you can ask for anything, politely.
“Noo suh-RYÕ”: the ending -rions, with a short i before the nasal on. Likewise “vous seriez” = “voo suh-RYAY”.
“Poo-ryay-voo”: the double r is read as one. But CAREFUL: “vous pouviez” (you could, imperfect) = “poo-vyay”, without r.
“Fee-ã-SY”: -ailles is read “eye”, as in “travail”. Ç = s.
The recipe is simple, and you already know half of it: the FUTURE STEM (ch. 19) + the IMPERFECT ENDINGS (ch. 13): -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.
All the verbs that are irregular in the future are irregular here too, with the same stem: j’irais, je ferais, je viendrais, je voudrais, je verrais, je saurais, je devrais, il faudrait.
Future vs conditional, with “je”: je serai (I will be) / je serais (I would be). In writing, the final “s” changes the whole meaning!
As in English (“I would like”, “could you”), the conditional makes a request more polite. It’s the basic reflex in shops, restaurants and the office:
I’d like to go to Iași.
Three ways of giving advice, from the most direct to the most delicate:
In your place, I’d take wine.
If I were you, I wouldn’t say anything.
It would be better to wait.
For an imaginary situation, French uses a fixed structure: SI + IMPARFAIT, then CONDITIONAL. Just like English (“if I had…, I would…”):
If I had time, I’d learn Japanese.
If her father said no, Julien would be sad.
If we lived by the sea, we’d swim every day.
NEVER use the conditional after SI: “Si j’avais” (not “si j’aurais”). It’s the classic mistake, even among French speakers!
S’il fait beau, on ira au parc.
S’il faisait beau, on irait au parc.
Careful: “belle-mère” means both mother-in-law and stepmother. “Beau-frère” = brother-in-law, “belle-sœur” = sister-in-law. The prefix beau-/belle- has nothing to do with beauty!

The following Wednesday, Julien went up to Fourvière alone. For a few weeks he had been going to see Hélène every Wednesday. He played for her on the old piano in the common room, and the other residents came to listen.
That day, after the music, Hélène said to him: “Come to my room. I’d like to show you something.”
She opened a drawer and took out a little blue velvet box, very worn. Inside there was a silver ring with a tiny green stone.
“Henri gave it to me on my twentieth birthday,” she explained. “He had no money. He had played the piano in cafés for six months to buy it. He told me: ‘When I come back, we’ll get engaged.’”
“I wore it for years. Then I put it away in this drawer. But I never gave it away, never sold it. I didn’t know why I was keeping it. Now I think I know.”
She put the little box in Julien’s hand. Julien didn’t understand. “Hélène, I could never accept…”
“Listen to me carefully,” said the old lady with a smile. “I’m not blind. I can see how you look at Ioana. If one day you wanted to ask her to marry you, I’d like her to wear this ring.”
“It would be as if Henri’s promise had finally been kept. Not for me. For the two of you.”

Julien looked at the ring for a long time. There were tears in his eyes. Then he confessed: “You know what? I was already thinking about it. I’d like to ask her in Iași this summer. But first I’d like to talk to her father.”
“Very good,” replied Hélène. “A well-brought-up young man. Henri would have done the same.”

She added, more seriously: “But be careful. If you said anything before the right moment, everything would be spoilt. The women in that family seem to guess everything. You’d have to hide the box very, very well.”
Julien laughed. “I’d hide it in my suitcase, among my scores. Ioana never looks at them. She says she doesn’t understand anything about written music.”
“Perfect. And what if her grandmother asked you why you looked so nervous?”
“I’d tell her it’s because of her cooking. Apparently she’s going to feed me for two weeks.”
Before he left, Hélène gave him one last piece of advice. “Don’t prepare a big speech. Henri prepared one, a very long one, and he forgot it completely. He just said: ‘Will you?’ And it was perfect.”
Julien promised to remember. He kissed her on both cheeks, the way you kiss a grandmother.

Going back down the hill, Julien was clutching the little blue box in his pocket. He was thinking of Henri, who had played in cafés for six months for this ring. He was thinking of Hélène, who had kept it for sixty-four years.
And he was thinking of Ioana, who was waiting for him at home, looking for train tickets to Iași on her computer. If she only knew, he thought with a smile. If only she knew…
